The Smartphone OS Knockout — 2006→2026 chart race.

0:00 Intro — what this race shows
0:30 2006–2009: Symbian & BlackBerry era
1:10 2010–2012: iPhone stabilizes, Android explodes

3:30 2021–2026: Modern duopoly and vanishing relics
4:10 Outro & key takeaways

Summary:
This visualization tracks global smartphone OS market share from 2006 through 2026. It shows one dramatic narrative: Android rises from effectively 0% to roughly 80%+ of global smartphone OS share, while long-time incumbents like Symbian and BlackBerry are effectively wiped out by the early 2010s. iOS grows steadily but never reaches the breadth of Android’s global footprint. Windows Mobile / Windows Phone fades after a brief period of relevance.

Why it matters:
This isn’t just a story about software — it’s platform economics, app ecosystems, carrier partnerships, developer mindshare, and hardware affordability. Android’s open model + low-cost hardware partners won the volume game; Apple kept premium margins and ecosystem control.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The OS that ate the smartphone world.

A decade and a half ago, Symbian and BlackBerry were the giants — Symbian controlled roughly 60% of the market in 2006, BlackBerry sat near 18%, and Android was basically nonexistent. Then everything changed. By 2011 Android had surged into the mainstream (about 50% global share that year); by 2014 it was past 75%. This visualization tracks that climb from zero to roughly 80%+ by the late 2010s — a platform-level takeover.

Why did Android win? Three brutal facts: (1) openness: Android allowed dozens of handset makers to ship cheap smartphones, flooding emerging markets; (2) ecosystem velocity: Google and partners built an app and services stack that developers embraced; (3) price coverage: Android’s low-end devices put smartphones within reach of billions.

Meanwhile, Symbian and BlackBerry collapsed. Nokia’s Symbian went from ~60% in 2006 to effectively 0% by 2014. BlackBerry’s share crashed from ~18% in 2006 to sub-1% by the mid-2010s. Windows Phone never recovered from late entry and fragmentation — it lingered briefly but then disappeared. Apple’s iOS didn’t die — it grew into a profitable and influential second pole (hovering mid-teens to high-teens % globally), but never matched Android’s sheer global footprint.

Key milestones: Android reaches ~50% by 2011; Symbian falls below 10% by 2012; BlackBerry becomes negligible by 2014; Android stabilizes around ~80% through the late 2010s and into the 2020s.

Which moment surprised you most — Android’s 2011 breakout or Symbian’s collapse? Tell me which year you remember switching phones and why.

Headline: The Smartphone OS Knockout — Android’s meteoric rise and the collapse of Symbian and BlackBerry.

From 2006 to 2026 the global smartphone operating system market was reshaped. Symbian controlled the majority of phones in 2006; by 2014 it had been all but erased. BlackBerry followed a similar path. Android, launched commercially in 2008, grew from near-0 to roughly 80%+ market share by the late 2010s, driven by an open platform model and low-cost hardware partners. Apple’s iOS consolidated the premium segment, hovering in the mid-to-high teens globally. The shift illustrates how platform openness, developer ecosystems, and hardware economics can reallocate global markets in a few short years.

Sources: StatCounter GlobalStats, IDC, Gartner, company reports, major press coverage.
